title: Putin Pushes New Russia-India Trade Corridor as Hormuz Crisis Bites
excerpt: Vladimir Putin says Russia is ready to finance the International North-South Transport Corridor with India and that Azerbaijan has agreed to its leg — but the project hinges on Iran completing its section.
body:
• Russian President Vladimir Putin said there is "very big potential" for economic cooperation with India beyond logistics, and that Moscow is talking to "our Indian friends" about jointly using new shipping and connectivity routes, including the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).
  • Russia is ready to fund the corridor's development — "we are prepared to provide loan financing... The necessary financial resources have been allocated" — but Putin said progress depends on Iran completing its section of the route.
  • The Azerbaijan leg is on track, Putin said: "We are in contact" with President Ilham Aliyev and "there are no problems there. Azerbaijan agrees."
  • The pitch comes as Iran's announced blockade of the Strait of Hormuz — following joint military strikes against Iran on February 28 — threatens shipments through a waterway carrying roughly 25% of global oil trade and 20% of LNG.

Putin's corridor pitch

Russian President Vladimir Putin has offered to deepen trade and transport links with India, saying there is "very big potential" for economic cooperation between the two countries that extends well beyond logistics. Speaking on October 1 about the development of global transport routes, Putin said Russia was actively discussing the joint use of new international shipping corridors with New Delhi, and that Moscow had already tested commercial vessels from China and South Korea.

"We have piloted a Chinese container ship and South Korean ship, and we are talking to our Indian friends as well," Putin said. "So we stand in favour of jointly using these promising international corridors."

At the centre of the proposal is the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), the long-discussed multimodal network linking Russia, Iran and India via Azerbaijan. Putin said Russia stands ready to provide the credit resources needed to develop the corridor — but added that the project does not depend on Moscow alone.

"Now, as far as the North-South transport corridor is concerned, it does not depend solely on us. We stand ready to provide the credit resources. But right now, our Iranian friends have to complete their part of the work."

— Vladimir Putin, President of Russia

Putin said the portion of the corridor passing through Azerbaijan was progressing without problems following his discussions with President Ilham Aliyev. "Part of the corridor must go through Azerbaijan, President Aliyev, and we are in contact. There are no problems there. Azerbaijan agrees," he said. In separate remarks, Putin added that Moscow was prepared to provide loan financing for the project and that "the necessary financial resources have been allocated for this purpose."

A waterway under blockade

The timing of Putin's remarks is tied to the escalating crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. On February 28, joint military strikes targeted key Iranian urban centres, including Tehran, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded with missile and drone operations against Israeli positions and US military bases across Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Tehran subsequently announced a maritime blockade of the Strait of Hormuz against vessels linked to the United States, Israel and allied nations.

The strait is one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints, accounting for approximately 25 per cent of global oil trade and nearly 20 per cent of worldwide liquefied natural gas shipments, according to News18. Any prolonged disruption threatens global energy prices and supply chains — which is why both Moscow and New Delhi are scrambling for alternatives.

Putin is not the first Russian official to link trade-route planning to Hormuz. In August, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said Moscow should examine the feasibility of a direct rail connection to the Indian Ocean to reduce transit risks tied to the Bosphorus and the Strait of Hormuz. "A rail link to the Indian Ocean should also be explored," Khusnullin told TASS, floating possible routes through Turkmenistan, Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

A two-decade-old project back in play

The INSTC is not a new idea. Russia, India and Iran conceived the corridor in the early 2000s and signed an intergovernmental agreement for a roughly 7,200 km multimodal transport corridor connecting India and Iran with Russia via rail, road and sea. For most of its life the project stalled: Western sanctions on Iran deterred investment, and before 2022 Moscow was reluctant to commit money while its relations with the West remained workable.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed that calculus. Western sanctions cut Moscow off from traditional European markets and trade routes, reviving interest in north-south connectivity. In May 2023, Russia and Iran signed a financing agreement for the Rasht-Astara railway link — the 170 km missing stretch on the corridor's western route — with Moscow footing most of the bill and completion targeted for 2027.

The economics are under pressure from another direction as well. The US has authorised tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian energy, raising the stakes for Moscow's energy trade with India, which has expanded sharply since 2022. Cheaper, more reliable freight routes would directly lower the cost of doing business between the two countries, which have set a bilateral trade target of $100 billion.

What it means for India and the diaspora

For India, the INSTC offers a shorter route to Russia and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan and the chokepoints of the Suez Canal. If operationalised, it could cut transit times and freight costs for Indian exporters in pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods — sectors that employ millions and anchor many diaspora-run trading businesses. For households, stable energy imports matter too: disruptions in Hormuz have a direct line to petrol and cooking-fuel prices in India, and an alternative overland corridor would reduce exposure to shipping insurance spikes that follow chokepoint crises.

There are diplomatic dividends as well. Alongside the corridor discussion, Putin praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi's efforts to seek a peaceful resolution to the Ukraine conflict, saying Modi has "very good ideas" for mutually acceptable solutions and had raised the issue despite the "very good and even friendly relations" between the two countries.

What to watch next

The real test is Iran. Putin's offer of Russian financing is only useful if Tehran completes its portion of the corridor — rail links, terminals and road networks that have been the project's bottleneck for decades. Watch for movement on the Rasht-Astara railway and any Iranian announcements on transit infrastructure in the coming months.

The second signal is New Delhi's formal response. India has shown interest in Russian connectivity projects — including, reportedly, the Northern Sea Route — and trade discussions run through the India-Russia intergovernmental commission, which last met in Moscow on August 24. Whether India commits capital or vessels to joint corridor use will show how far Putin's "very big potential" translates into policy. Until then, the corridor remains what it has been for twenty years: a promising blueprint waiting on Iran.
